title: Kedoshim: holiness for everyone (Leviticus 19:2)
hook: holiness is spoken to the whole congregation, not only to priests

segments.voice: Yesterday, pikuach nefesh: the law is for living. Your line was live by them. Did you do the one thing your body needed? Today, a new portion, and maybe the most quoted chapter in Leviticus. Day four hundred ten.

For most of Leviticus, holiness has had a dress code. Linen garments, a golden plate, a turban. It's had an address: the sanctuary, the altar, the room behind the curtain. And it's had a short guest list: Aaron, his sons, a high priest once a year. If you were a shepherd or a weaver or a kid in the camp, holiness was something you watched from the courtyard. Then chapter nineteen opens, and the guest list changes completely.
screen: `HOLINESS HAD A DRESS CODE.` → `AND A SHORT GUEST LIST.` → `CHAPTER NINETEEN CHANGES IT.`

segments.voice: First, the address. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Speak unto all the congregation of the children of Israel, and say unto them: Ye shall be holy; for I the LORD your God am holy." All the congregation. Not the priests. Everyone. The portion takes its name from that call: Kedoshim, holy ones. Second, the assembly. Rashi, drawing on an older midrash, says this chapter was taught with the whole people gathered together, because most of the essentials of the Torah depend on it. Third, what holy looks like here. Read on, and the chapter doesn't send anyone to the altar. Revere your mother and your father. Keep the Sabbath. Don't steal, don't lie to each other. Pay a hired worker the same day; don't keep his wages overnight. Rise before the gray head and honor the old. Keep honest scales and honest weights. Holiness, in Kedoshim, sits in a paycheck, a grocery scale, a seat given up on the bus. Fourth, the mix. The chapter switches back and forth between what we'd call ritual and what we'd call ethics, sometimes verse to verse, and never marks the difference. Many teachers say that's the point. The holy and the decent aren't two departments. Over the next days we'll take a few of these verses one at a time. For today, just the opening: the call is to everyone, and it lands in ordinary places.
screen: `ALL THE CONGREGATION.` · `TAUGHT TO THE WHOLE ASSEMBLY.` · `WAGES, SCALES, THE GRAY HEAD.` · `RITUAL AND ETHICS, UNMARKED.` · then, large: `YE SHALL BE HOLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one ordinary thing in a holy way. Settle, and breathe. Pick something from your day that's completely ordinary. Paying someone. Answering an email. Giving change at the register. Cooking dinner. Picture doing it as though it were part of a holy day: careful, honest, on time, with attention to the person on the other end. Not slower, necessarily. Just set apart. Choose which one you'll do that way today. The bell holds the time.
Kedoshim. Holy ones: the portion that calls the whole people to holiness, and finds it in wages, scales and honoring the old.
Your line: holiness for everyone. Today, do the ordinary thing you chose as carefully as a priest would. Day four hundred ten.

howItsDone: Kedoshim is read in synagogue in the spring, often together with Acharei Mot, and Leviticus 19 is among the chapters most studied and taught in Jewish ethics.

fork.setup: you're a hired laborer in the camp. you finish a day's work at sunset. when does Leviticus 19 say you get paid?
options: at the end of the week.
that same day, not kept overnight.
fork.reveal: the wages shall not stay with the employer all night until morning. holiness, in Kedoshim, includes the paycheck.

original.note: Hebrew: "you shall be holy" (Leviticus 19:2), the words that name the portion.

what it means: the call to be holy goes to everyone, and is lived in ordinary dealings.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on 19:2, from the Sifra, says the chapter was taught be-hakhel, in full assembly, because most of the Torah's essentials hang on it.

Verses summarized: parents and Sabbath (19:3), not stealing or lying (19:11), wages not held overnight (19:13), rising before the aged (19:32), honest weights (19:35–36). 'A seat given up on the bus' is a modern image.
